title: Asa Seeks the LORD and Defeats Zerah
summary: Asa succeeds Abijah and does what is good and right: he removes foreign altars, high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles, and he commands Judah to seek the LORD. God gives the land ten years of rest, which Asa uses to fortify cities. When Zerah the Cushite invades with a vast army, Asa cries out to the LORD for help, and God routs the invaders, who are pursued as far as Gerar.
story: Abijah's single battle showed Judah relying on the LORD (chapter 13). His son Asa receives the longest treatment of any king so far after Solomon, across chapters 14 to 16, and his reign is told as a story in two halves: many years of seeking God, then a late turn toward self-reliance. This chapter shows the first half at its best. Reform leads to rest, rest to building, and a crisis to a prayer that is one of the finest in the book. The victory here is followed in chapter 15 by a prophet's word and a covenant renewal.
historical:
Asa reigned forty-one years, about 911 to 870 BC. The books of Kings summarize his reign in 1 Kings 15:9-24, praising his removal of idols and noting his war with Baasha of Israel, but Kings does not mention the invasion of Zerah, which appears only in Chronicles. Zerah is called a Cushite, and he has not been identified with certainty in any record outside the Bible. Some scholars have suggested he was a commander serving the Egyptian pharaoh Osorkon I, Shishak's successor; others think he led Cushite groups settled in the southern border region, since the battle ends near Gerar and the plunder includes tents, sheep, and camels, the property of herders rather than a pharaoh's army. The text does not call him a king.

Mareshah, where the armies met, was one of the fortified towns Rehoboam built (11:8), on the western approach to Judah in the low hills of the Shephelah. The Valley of Zephathah is otherwise unknown. Gerar lay to the southwest, in the western Negev toward Gaza, the region where Abraham and Isaac had once lived (Genesis 20 and 26). In English Bibles 14:1 corresponds to 13:23 in the Hebrew text, so verse numbers in this chapter differ by one between Hebrew and English editions.
cultural:
Asa's reform targets the standard features of Canaanite religion. Foreign altars served gods other than the LORD. High places were hilltop or local shrines; some were used to worship the LORD himself, but the law called for sacrifice at the one place God would choose (Deuteronomy 12), and the high places easily blended Israel's worship with its neighbors'. Sacred pillars were standing stones associated with a deity. Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and the Asherah poles were wooden cult objects representing her, often set up beside altars. The incense altars of verse 5 may be small altars used in local worship.

The description of Asa's troops reflects real divisions of an ancient army. Men of Judah carried large shields and spears, suited to close formation fighting, while men of Benjamin carried small shields and bows, the lighter arms of skirmishers. Benjamin was known for its archers and slingers (1 Chronicles 8:40, 12:2). A king in the ancient world was expected to build walls and store cities, and here the building happens because God has given rest, not as a substitute for trusting him.
literary: The chapter has two movements, peace and war, joined by the key verb seek. Verses 1 to 8 are built from repeated statements of rest and quiet: the land was at peace (verses 1, 5, 6), and the LORD gave rest on every side (verses 6 and 7). Asa's short speech in verse 7 draws the lesson in his own words: "We have sought Him and He has given us rest on every side." Verses 9 to 15 then test that confidence with an army far larger than Judah's. Asa's prayer in verse 11 is the center of the second half: it confesses that no one besides God can help the powerless, asks for help, states reliance, and appeals to God's own honor. The outcome is told briefly, and verse 13 names the army as the LORD's own.

outline.t: Asa becomes king and removes idolatrous worship
Rest, fortified cities, and Asa's army
The LORD routs the Cushites, and Judah takes the plunder

doctrines.note: Asa's prayer in verse 11 is a model of dependence: it names God's unique power to help the weak, asks directly for help, confesses reliance, and places the outcome in terms of God's own name. Prayer here is not a last resort but the natural speech of a king who has been seeking God.
Seeking the LORD begins with clearing away rival worship. Asa's reform shows that faithfulness has a concrete, public shape: altars, pillars, and poles removed.
Rest is presented as God's gift, not merely a lull in foreign politics. The same God who gives rest also defends his people when the rest is broken.

words.note: Darash, to seek, inquire of, or resort to. This is the Chronicler's master word for true religion, used three times in this chapter. It includes worship, prayer, and obedience, and it describes a whole life oriented toward God. Asa commands it, the people practice it, and he credits Judah's peace to it.

Nuach, to rest. Rest is a covenant gift in the Old Testament, promised when Israel entered the land (Deuteronomy 12:10) and given to Solomon, the man of rest (1 Chronicles 22:9). Asa's rest shows God keeping that promise to a faithful king.

Azar, to help. The verb frames Asa's prayer: there is no one besides God to help, so help us. The name of God as helper runs through the Psalms, and here it defines the relationship between a weak king and a strong God.

Sha'an, to lean or rely on. Asa says, for we rely on You. The Chronicler will use this very verb again in chapter 16, when Asa relies on the king of Aram instead of the LORD, and the contrast between the two uses is the story of Asa's life.

christ: Asa's prayer confesses that God helps the powerless against the mighty, and that confession runs through the whole Bible until it reaches its fullest expression in the gospel. Mary sings that God has brought down rulers and lifted up the humble (Luke 1:52), and Paul says God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27). In Christ, God fought the decisive battle on behalf of people who could not win it themselves, not with an army but through the cross and resurrection (Colossians 2:15). The connection is thematic: Asa is not a picture of Christ, but his prayer expresses the dependence that the gospel calls for.

hard.q: How should we read a million-man army and a war that ends in plundering towns and herders' tents?
hard.a:
The army of a million is the largest figure in Chronicles, and readers approach it in the same ways as the numbers in chapter 13: as literal, as counting units rather than individuals (since eleph can mean a clan or military unit), or as a conventional way of saying an overwhelming force. The Chronicler's concern is the contrast between human weakness and God's help, which the numbers dramatize.

The plundering of the cities around Gerar and the herdsmen's camps is reported without comment, as ordinary ancient warfare, in which an invading force's base and supply towns were fair targets. The text attributes it to the terror of the LORD falling on those cities, which suggests they were linked with Zerah's invasion. Readers today rightly feel the weight of such scenes. The Chronicler presents the war as defense against an invader, not as a model for how God's people should treat others, and the rest of Scripture sets the violence of Israel's wars within a larger story that ends in the peace of God's kingdom.

questions: Asa used peaceful years to build and prepare. What might it look like to use a quiet season in your life to strengthen your trust in God?
Asa prayed, “there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty.” Where do you feel powerless now, and what would it mean to pray that way?
Removing idols came before the rest and the victory. What rival loyalties would need to come down in your life for you to seek God wholeheartedly?
